Amaria had heard of them, of course. Everyone had. Their names whispered in market stalls, their deeds dissected in grim news reports—always deaths, never injuries.They were efficient, terrifying. A string of wreckage left in their wake, punctuated only by an ever-rising bounty, a number so absurd it had taken on an almost mythical quality. Their faces were everywhere, plastered across warning screens, staring out from grainy wanted posters with the ominous, unambiguous warning: DANGEROUS. DO NOT ENGAGE.

And yet, as she stood behind the cake stand in her tiny patisserie, watching them bicker over a plate of lemon tarts, it was almost impossible to reconcile the men before her with the ghosts of those reports.

The Tempest—deadliest mage in a hundred systems—currently had cookie crumbs clinging to his chin. The Siren—the cold-blooded strategist who had taken down an entire warship single-handed—was leaning over, dabbing them away with the kind of patient fondness that made Amaria’s chest ache.

She wouldn’t call them regulars. Their visits were sporadic at best, sometimes months apart, yet somehow, they always found their way back to her little shop at the edge of the universe. The blue one—the Tempest—always ordered with that same easy charm, rattling off their choices with a grin that made her fingers twitch. The cakes varied—clearly, they were making their way through the menu—but the drinks? Always the same. Black coffee for the Tempest. Sweet lemonade for the Siren.

At first, she had been terrified. Hands trembling as she placed their tray down, gaze darting to the blade at the Siren’s hip. But then she had watched them. Really watched them. The way they spoke in low, conspiratorial murmurs, heads bent close over their shared desserts. The way the Siren would casually steal bites from the Tempest’s plate, and the Tempest—who by all accounts had decimated a Capital legion in a single evening—would only sigh and let him.

It was hard to remain scared after that.

Not everyone saw it that way, of course.

One time, the moment they left, Leggy Wilbur—so named for his tragically high-waisted pants, which made his already long legs appear comically endless—waddled over, eyes wide, lips pursed with barely contained scandal. He jerked his chin toward the old screen in the corner, currently droning on about tax reform in the Capital. But there, at the bottom of the screen, rolling along like an afterthought, was the number. That staggering, life-altering bounty.

Amaria heard his voice, thick with a mix of outrage and greedy curiosity.

"That’s them. That’s them," he hissed, voice pitched low but urgent.

She shrugged, wiping down the counter.

The bounty was tempting, sure. Enough money to rewrite her life entirely. But here, out on the edge of the galaxy, where the only thing the Capital ever gave them was rising taxes and dwindling bank balances, Amaria had long since decided where her loyalty lay.

So, she supported them in the ways that mattered.

She made the lemonade fresh. She picked the warmest cookies.

And she let them be.

.

It was, without question, the most dangerous fight they’d ever faced.

Frey’s nerves thrummed like over-tightened bowstrings as he kept his gaze flicking across the battlefield. Brian Styles clung to the undead roc’s jagged spine, carving through fossil-hard bone and scooping out rotting viscera with the implacable calm only he could manage. Star darted in and out beneath the creature’s wingspan, his hammer landing bone-shaking blows before he retreated again, bloody but unbowed.

And Jun—
Jun was doing his best impression of a terrified mole, slipping in and out of his snow hole as though the ground itself were his ally. Every few seconds Frey caught a shock of blue skin, the rainbow shimmer of Jun’s cowl, the crackle of familiar magic—and then Jun vanished below the surface again, too fragile to risk exposure after the force-field incident. He was smart to hide. Frey told himself that. But it didn’t stop the little twist of fear in his gut every time Jun disappeared from view.

Frey could feel his spell straining, tugging at the very core of him. Earthbind held the roc to the ground, but barely—the magic dragged at him with the weight of the creature’s fury. The beast fought like a hurricane. But the spell held. They were hurting it. They might actually live.

Then the arrow hit.

It hissed through the air and buried itself in Frey’s shoulder with a wet, meaty thud. A sickening burn pulsed outward from the wound, unnatural and cold, seeping down his arm and creeping up the side of his neck. His breath hitched. He snapped his head toward the mountainside—figures, human-shaped silhouettes in furs, half-lost in the whiteout. His mind whispered yeti? goliaths? cultists? but he couldn’t spare a second look.

If he faltered, if the spell broke, the roc would be free. And they would die.

Gritting his teeth, Frey slid up and out of his snow-burrow, moving low and fast. His feet skidded across ice as he dashed thirty-five feet to the next cover, sliding into the hollow and pressing his back against frozen stone. The cold bit at his skin, shockingly sharp, but he forced himself to ignore it. He balled his fist, focused, and sent a spear of psychic force stabbing into the roc’s primitive mind. The gargantuan bird shrieked, jerking its head back, stunned with pain.

Good, Frey thought. Focus. Kill the roc first. Deal with whatever’s shooting next.

Then a shout cracked the air.

Jun’s magic rippled outward—wild, unpredictable, terrifying. Frey whipped his head toward him just as the world above Jun exploded into shimmering water. Torrents crashed down into the hole where he hid, filling it in seconds with frigid melt.

“Jun!” Frey hissed.

A drenched shape scrambled free, coughing, blue skin blanched nearly grey with cold. Jun’s hair clung to his face in sodden strands, his eyes were wide with shock. Panic hollowed his features, real and raw.

He staggered toward Frey.

“Come on,” Frey breathed, reaching out, heart pounding. He wanted—gods, he wanted—to pull Jun into safety, into his arms if he could get away with it.

But he never got the chance.

With a sound like mountains shattering, the roc tore one wing free of the goliath-held restraint. Then the other. The massive limbs snapped open and slammed down against the earth.

The shockwave blasted through the snowfield.

Frey ducked instinctively, horns scraping stone as the impact roared over his head. Ice and wind hit him like a thrown wall. He held firm. The moment it passed he thrust his head back up—

—and his breath vanished.

“Jun?”

The elf lay sprawled on the ground, thrown like a ragdoll. Limbs tangled. White hair fanned over the snow like spilled silk. His eyes were closed, lips parted, a thin line of blood trailing from the corner of his mouth.

Frey’s heart stopped, then crashed against his ribs with brutal force.

“Oh no.”
His voice came out a whisper, fragile as frost.

Jun wasn’t moving.

“Well, it hurts.” He said thoughtfully, “but not any more than I’d expected, and other than that, I feel fine?” He uttered the words with a hint of disbelief, as though he couldn't trust the words coming out of his own mouth. Frey's heart skipped a beat and a fragile ember of hope ignited within him against all odds.

“Who knows, between us you’re normally the one with the, oogly boogly,'' Frey joked, wiggling his fingers above his head, “Maybe you’re immune? I’ve heard of a few cases where people have been bit and haven’t turned.” Jun's smile, although fragile, mirrored Frey's flicker of hope, and he clung to it desperately.

“Yeah, hopefully…”

Frey lost time. His arms, raised high above his head in a tight stretch, were killing him. The steel manacles cut into his wrist and there was no give. He couldn’t lower his arms an inch, which forced him to stand up straight which then made his back ache, and his knees, and his feet. Oh, he hurt.

“Frey?” Through the haze of his own suffering, he heard Jun's voice, ragged and strained, calling out to him. Frey's eyes snapped to his lover, and his heart sank like a stone in the pit of his stomach.

Beads of sweat were coalescing at Jun’s hairline and his eyes were red rimmed and sore looking. The sight of Jun's suffering was a gut-wrenching blow.

“I don’t think I’m immune.” Jun confessed, his voice heavy with despair. Frey felt as if the ground had crumbled beneath him. The fragile glimmer of hope they had clung to, no matter how faint, flickered and was extinguished, leaving them with the dread reality they couldn't escape.

Jun was dying. And Frey was going to watch it happen, slowly, painfully, within arms reach but unable to hold him. He was condemned to stand helplessly by, unable to offer anything more than his anguished presence.

Frey paused for a moment, his own tears glistening in his eyes, but he refused to let despair overtake him. "Then I'll close my eyes," he promised. He would do whatever it took to protect Jun, even if it meant facing the unthinkable blindly.

Frey's heart clenched as he watched Jun's frail form, his lover's body ravaged by pain and suffering. He sniffed, trying to stamp down the terror threatening to claw out his throat. His voice quivered as he spoke, trying to be the source of strength that Jun so desperately needed. “You don’t have to hold on for me.”

With every ounce of strength he could muster, Frey leaned forward, straining against the unyielding restraints, his arms protesting in agony. He pressed a kiss to Jun’s sweat soaked cheek. “Jun, It’s okay.” He reassured, though the lie hung heavily in the air.

Jun's gasping sobs wracked his fragile frame, each breath clearly a torturous struggle. His bloodshot, sore eyes pleaded with Frey, and his ashen skin spoke of the torment he endured.

“Don’t be, love. Rest now. I’ll see you in the next one.” he whispered, his voice barely holding steady.Jun mustered a pained half-smile, his strength waning with each passing moment. His eyes, once vibrant, now dulled with exhaustion and fever, began to drift closed. Finally, achingly, slowly, his head fell forward, and he sagged limply in the chains. A final, heart-wrenching breath escaped Jun's lips, so soft and fragile it was almost inaudible.

It was over. Jun was at peace now, and Frey's heart shattered into a million pieces.

"I'll see you soon," Frey whispered into the silent, desolate room, his voice filled with a mix of resignation and heartache. He closed his eyes and braced himself for the inevitable.

The atmosphere in the Wicker Goat was warm, friendly and inviting. A far cry from the ethereal and alien realm they had just escaped from. They had been in the fey realm for close to a week, and yet, here in Saltmarsh, two months had passed!

They had become quite close in their own company, the four of them, Frey, Jun, Brian Styles and Star, so it felt a little bit jarring for Jun, when Star waved them off and left to do his own thing. Jun watched him go and felt a little wary, struggling to reacclimate himself to a world that wasn’t incredibly dangerous.

Eddie, thankfully had not changed, except that the lines that had begun forming on his face whilst they were embroiled in the war against the sahuagin had faded after two months of peace. Clearly he was much happier spending time in the town, and was rather unsuited to cold campfires and wet bedrolls. Patrons of the inn were clearly familiar with him, and he smiled and called them by name as they promised to visit his stall on the next market day.

Frey seemed much happier as well when he was in the wizard’s company, there was a new looseness to his posture that hadn’t been present when they were in the feydark. Whether that was because of the ever-present danger, or the strange new company, Jun couldn’t tell. It was nice to see the tiefling let loose however, his jokes had a different weight to them here. He and Eddie had a closeness borne of years of knowing each other, and the humour was much lighter, instead of the meanspiritedness and jabs that had been present amongst the four of them.

The group claimed a table in the corner, and Jun sat in the corner with his back to the wall. Although the townsfolk greeted him warmly he still felt rather self-conscious, especially now he was the brightest thing in the room. He was enamoured with his new cowl, but it was rather… vibrant, and he wasn’t quite used to wearing clothing that wasn’t his customary black or dark blue. Still, he’d received some compliments, and one rather forward woman had clasped him by the hand and told him the cloak made his violet eyes appear “simply incandescent”. Jun had thanked her and politely ignored Frey’s snort of laughter.

Frey loudly insisted that Eddie buy the first round, to which the lizard obliged, and four glasses of strong peach-smelling spirits were served. Jun was content to fade into the background of the conversation as Frey and Eddie reconnected. He was happy to take a backseat to Frey’s animated retelling of their encounters in the feywild, from the consuming fire that forced them there, to slaying a dragon, losing Fizzy… inciting a rebellion amongst cyclops’, making friends with a firbolg (‘and her pig, Morel’ Brian Styles interjected). Frey waxed lyrically about the pool of jellyfish, to which Eddie responded by getting out his smoke pipe and claiming it wasn't such a big deal. Then he spoke about how they slew the wizard who was ‘pinned to the tree! Like it was part of him! Then Brian Styles put the super cursed shard in a box. He’s still got it!’

Then Frey got to the part about the Deer lord, “And get this Eddie, the deer lord is the one giving Jun all his magic, and apparently that necklace he left with you is possibly the most dangerous thing in the world, because some evil goddess wants it, and she’s hunting Jun down to get it back. You’re lucky she didn’t kill you when we left!” Frey laughed and took another bite of his bread.

Eddie looked to Jun, but Jun wouldn’t meet his eyes.

“I’m sorry,” the elf said, “I knew it was dangerous, which is why I didn’t risk taking it to the Feywild, but it was stupid to leave it with you.”

The lizard wizard’s eyes circled as he thought carefully for a moment.

“Well, you paid me handsomely for it, so I don’t mind!” Jun raised an eyebrow,

“But I didn’t pay you- you stole…! Ah,” The lizard winked at him and Jun cocked one side of his mouth in a wry smile.

Brian Styles interjected at this point that they still had to retrieve their shadows and Fizzy, which prompted Eddie and Frey to weigh up the cost-benefits in doing so.

Jun sat silently as his thoughts took him elsewhere. It had literally only been a few hours since he had spoken to the Deer Lord. The being who he owed his continued life to. The being who told him he would forever be hunted. Was that why his life had been saved, because he served a purpose of protecting the gem? Was this the entire reason for his existence, his magic, his ‘dream touched’ status? What did this mean for his future?

Was he doomed to continue his nomadic life, always on the run from some being who he couldn’t see, a literal shadow hounding his steps. What did that mean to the people around him? Although he’d only been with them a few months he’d become exceptionally fond of these strange characters who had invited him to travel, work, eat, and fight with them.

Jun had even stopped flinching whenever he heard voices when he woke up, because he had grown used to no longer waking up alone. The constant chattering and bickering had become home to him, and was he willing to give that up?

Star, Fizzy, Brian Styles, Eddie, Frey, even Loke and Erneaster… They had been kind to him and treated him as an ally.

How was he supposed to continue putting them in danger by his mere presence? He knew the safest option for them was to slip away, to leave Saltmarsh behind and keep moving.

Alone.

But, was he strong enough to leave?

In front of him, Eddie had pulled out a scrap of parchment and a quill and was drawing some kind of diagram with a crude picture of Fizzy on one side and a pile of coins on the other. Frey was laughing, his rose cheeks flushed from the spirits that he’d insisted keep coming to the table.

Beside them Brian Styles had leaned over to add his deadpan comments. He slid the parchment across to himself and drew an inexplicably detailed trebuchet on it with an arrow connecting the two other pictures. Eddie’s eyes whirled in bewilderment causing Frey to burst into harder laughter, his shaggy white hair falling forward, covering his eyes creased in mirth. Jun felt an odd compulsion to sweep the hair to one side…

No. Jun wasn’t strong enough to leave.

Hold on, I'm coming for you
Just tell me where to go and I'll come running for you
Chapter One
Frey woke up, feeling more rested than he had in weeks. For once, the weight of their quest seemed distant, and he was almost tempted to stay in bed. The goliaths sure knew how to make a good mattress—the mountain-bred feathers packed into the bedrolls made it feel like he was floating. He stretched, rolling his shoulders and flicking the kinks out of his tail, then layered on the furs that shielded him from the biting cold outside.
Four days until the world ended. Plenty of time for breakfast.
With a light step and a grin, Frey headed to the communal food hall, where the scent of roasted meat and sweet milk from last night still lingered in the air. As expected, Star and Brian Styles were already there, tucked in a corner. Their isolation from the rest of the goliaths was noticeable, but Star seemed to take it in stride. Brian Styles, on the other hand, looked more introspective than usual.
Frey slid into a seat with a flourish, snatching a crusty roll from Star’s plate and biting into it before Star could react.
“You know I licked that, right?” Star said, his voice low but amused.
Frey’s eye twitched mid-chew. “Aww, Star. Now it’s like I’ve kissed you. Guess I know what you taste like.” He shot him a wink, his grin wide.
Star groaned, and Brian Styles quietly slid a plate of food toward Frey. “Saved you some,” he said with his usual calm.
Frey’s grin softened into something genuine. “Thanks, Brian Styles.” He dug into the plate, tearing into the food like he hadn’t eaten in days. Between bites, he asked, “So, what’s the plan? Kidnap that yeti you suggested, Star? Or scout around the mountain some more?”
Brian Styles opened his mouth to respond, but Frey cut him off, still chewing. “On second thought, shouldn’t we wait for Jun before we decide anything? You know he’s bound to have an opinion.”
The silence that followed was so abrupt it almost felt tangible. Both Star and Brian Styles were staring at him, blank-faced.
“What?” Frey swallowed, eyebrows raised. “Don’t tell me Jun’s still soaking in that bath. He’s going to shrivel up like a prune.”
Star’s brow furrowed. “Who?”
Frey blinked, his stomach tightening. “Jun? You know, our little blue elf who overthinks everything and gets blasted to hell every other day? You’re messing with me, right?”
Star shook his head slowly, his expression growing serious. “Frey, you feeling alright? You hit your head?”
Brian Styles’ voice was careful. “I don’t recall anyone by that name.”
Frey’s pulse quickened. He pushed back from the table, the stool scraping loudly against the stone floor. “This isn’t funny. We’re the Four Essences. Me, Star, Brian Styles, and Jun.”
Star exchanged a glance with Brian Styles, then said, “You, me, Brian Styles, and Arnie. That’s it.”
“No.” Frey felt like the air was being squeezed out of his chest. “No, no, no.” His voice trembled as he spoke. “I’ll prove it. I’ll be right back.”
He bolted from the hall, sprinting through the snow to the tent where Jun had stayed the night before. His hands shook as he tore open the heavy flap, but the inside was empty—nothing but crates of supplies and bottles. No bed. No evidence of Jun. No trace that he’d ever been there.
“What the hell…” Frey whispered, backing out of the tent in disbelief. His heart raced, panic swelling in his chest. He stumbled through the snow, his mind reeling.
Brian Styles followed him outside, his expression unreadable. “Frey?” he asked quietly. “What’s going on?”
Frey spun around, eyes wild. “Where is he? How can you not remember? Jun’s been with us from the start! We crossed the Fey Realm together, fought side by side—he’s real!”
Brian Styles frowned, his normally steady gaze faltering. “Could it have been a vision? You’ve been through a lot—”
“No!” Frey shouted, his voice cracking. He dropped to his knees in the snow, scrambling through his pack until his fingers closed around the teapot. He yanked it out, shaking as he focused on the swirling jellyfish within. “Show me,” he pleaded. “Show me Jun.”
The jellyfish shimmered, swirling in response to his memories. It revealed the group—twelve huskies, a blue goliath, a warforged, a woman, a tiefling, and a tiger. Frey watched as they climbed the snowy peaks of Rokoss. But there was no Jun. No blue elf. His face paled.
“Please,” Frey begged, his voice breaking. He rifled through memory after memory, each one cruelly confirming the same truth—Jun wasn’t there.
A hand rested gently on his shoulder, but Frey shook it off, his breath coming in shallow gasps. “It’s the barrier,” he muttered, panic bubbling in his throat. “Ikoran… Ikoran must’ve done something. Star said they hate magic users here. What if they erased him? What if—”
His voice faltered, breaking into ragged silence as Brian Styles crouched beside him, his presence quiet but steady.
“Frey,” he said softly. “We’ll figure it out. But you need to breathe.”
Frey’s chest heaved as the weight of it all hit him. He sat there in the snow, clutching the teapot, as the world seemed to shrink around him. The biting cold was nothing compared to the gaping emptiness in his heart.
Because somewhere, deep down, Frey knew.
Jun was gone. And somehow, he was the only one who remembered.

Chapter Two

“You must know something! What have you done with him?” Frey’s voice cracked, laced with fury, as Star and Brian Styles stood behind him. The air in the tent felt thick with tension, the cold seeping through the fabric as Ikoran, the Rokoss shaman, scowled defensively.
“Stargazer, I’ve been patient, but your group is making accusations I don’t appreciate.” His voice was calm, but there was an edge to his words. Star let out a heavy sigh.
“Frey, we’ve questioned everyone in the village,” Star said, his tone measured, trying to maintain some semblance of calm. “Nobody knows anything about this... Jon.”
Frey’s eyes flashed with anger. “It’s Jun!” He snapped, his frustration boiling over. “And I’m not giving up!” Without another word, he stormed out of the tent, snow crunching under his boots. The others exchanged a glance before following him out into the bitter cold.
Star caught up to him first. “Look, Frey, maybe…” he began, choosing his words carefully, “maybe you just dreamt it. We’ve got bigger things to worry about right now.”
Frey spun on his heel, eyes blazing with fury. “Bigger than our friend who’s missing?” His voice broke slightly at the end, betraying the emotion he was fighting to suppress. His throat tightened, his eyes burning. Why didn’t they believe him?
Brian Styles stepped forward, his calm voice cutting through the rising tension. “For what purpose would this happen now? There are two possibilities here,” he said, holding his hands up before Frey could cut him off. “One, you’ve been led to believe we had another companion, some trick of the mind—” He paused, seeing Frey’s glare darken. “I’m not saying that’s true, Frey. But the other possibility is that one of us has been taken—and for some reason, you’re the only one who remembers.”
Frey’s resolve wavered as he sat down heavily in the snow, putting his head in his hands. “If you’ve ever believed anything I’ve said, believe this,” he said, his voice thick with emotion. “I wouldn’t imagine someone like Jun. He’s... he’s frustrating, he’s reckless, he’s pretty much useless in a fight, and he argues with us over everything.”
Star crossed his arms, brow furrowed. “Then maybe it’s better he’s gone?” He half-joked, trying to lighten the mood. But the sharp glare Frey shot him made him wince.
Frey’s voice softened. “But he’s also good. He doesn’t run when things get tough. He might not fight like us, but he tries to keep us safe. He’s a good man, and I’m not leaving him behind.”
Star sighed and sat down next to Frey in the snow, his expression shifting to something more serious. “Alright. We believe you,” he said, his voice low. “Now we just have to figure out who took him and why. And, you know, save the world in four days. No big deal.” He cracked a half-smile, trying to pull Frey out of his despair.
Brian Styles nodded thoughtfully. “You said Jun was one of the Four Essences, right? Maybe that’s why he was targeted—to weaken the group. Separate us.”
Frey’s eyes lit up with a glimmer of hope. “Yeah… yeah, maybe! It makes sense.” He jumped to his feet, energy returning. “We need to check the barrier again! Jun got blasted by it yesterday, maybe it affected him in some way.” He was already walking, determination driving his steps as the three of them headed back up toward the peak.
The clear, spherical barrier shimmered in the distance, just as it had the day before. Frey approached it cautiously, his heart pounding. The runes etched into the surface were as incomprehensible as ever, and frustration gnawed at him. He clenched his fists, banging one against the invisible wall. Nothing happened.
“It has to be this,” he muttered, anger building. “It’s the only thing that makes sense!”
A soft voice interrupted his thoughts. “The villagers said you were up here. Is everything alright?” Rayra’s voice was gentle as she approached, her steps slow and cautious. Brian Styles turned to her and gave a polite nod.
“It appears we’ve lost one of our companions,” he said, his voice as neutral as ever.
Rayra’s brow furrowed, genuine confusion crossing her face. “What do you mean?” she asked, glancing between them.
Star shrugged. “Frey says we were travelling with a magic-wielding elf but they’ve gone missing and none of us can remember for some reason.”
Frey nodded, but the fight had drained from his posture. Exhausted, he just stared at the ground, too tired to argue. He wasn’t sure if he had the energy to explain it all again.
Rayra looked at him with soft sympathy. “I’m not sure what I can do, but I’ll help in any way I can to get him back.”
Frey’s breath caught in his throat. Something felt… wrong. His eyes snapped up to meet hers. She looked startled by the intensity in his gaze.
“What did you just say?” Frey asked, his voice low and dangerous.
Rayra blinked, confused. “I said I’d help.”
“No,” Frey stepped closer, his pulse quickening. “You said ‘him.’”
Her expression faltered, eyes darting between Frey and the others. “What do you mean?”
Frey’s heart pounded in his chest as fiery energy began to spark at his fingertips. “We never mentioned that Jun was male.”
Brian Styles and Star immediately went on alert, stepping forward and unsheathing their weapons as Rayra stumbled back, eyes wide with fear. But something shifted in her demeanour. Her expression morphed from surprise to something darker, her lips curling into a slow, playful smirk.
“Ah,” she said, her voice dropping to a teasing tone. “You caught me.”
Frey took a step back, his fiery energy crackling more violently around his fingers. Star and Brian Styles held their weapons at the ready, while Rayra’s smirk deepened, her eyes gleaming with something dark and predatory.
“What did you do to him?” Frey growled, his voice low and dangerous.
Rayra tilted her head slightly, her expression almost mocking. “This is a shame, you are a complication, little bard.” She fixed Frey with a smile, “why is it the memory spell didn’t hold on you… Could it be, you’re connected?” She glanced around, the snow crunching under her feet as she slowly circled them, almost leisurely.
“Enough games,” Star said, his hand tightening around the hilt of his sword. “Tell us where Goon is, or this gets ugly.”

Chapter Three
Frey fell. Or rather, he plummeted through a whirlpool of sensations, colours, and endless movement. There was no sense of time—seconds, hours, days—it all bled together in a rush of stars and galaxies, oceans and landscapes, all swirling around him in a kaleidoscope of chaos. His body twisted through the cosmos, as if the very fabric of reality was unravelling around him.
And then he stopped.
The stillness was jarring, leaving him suspended in nothingness, as though he were under a slow-falling flight spell. His breath was the only sound in the silence. Frey blinked, trying to orient himself, but all he saw was an endless expanse of doors. Grand oak doors, gleaming silver doors, doors made of twisted vines and wrought iron. Thousands—no, millions of them. Each unique. Each leading somewhere unknown.
Jun was behind one of these. Frey gritted his teeth. Impossible, Rayra had said. Well, he’d show her what impossible looked like.
He took a deep breath and reached out for the first door.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Frey woke up. His head spun for a moment, disoriented by the shift. He was no longer free-falling through space, nor was he surrounded by cold winds or snow. Instead, he was warm. Too warm. He opened his eyes to find himself in a small, grey room—confined and stark. It reminded him of a prison cell he’d been in once, though this one was far stranger. The walls were smooth and cold, but the bedding beneath him was an unexpected lavender, embroidered with delicate patterns of flowers and spirals. It felt absurd in the sterile surroundings.
Frey pushed himself up, his senses struggling to catch up. The clothes he had been wearing—his furs, his travel gear—were gone, replaced with a one-piece suit made of a slick, unfamiliar fabric that clung to his body. It covered him from his neck down, strange and alien in its feel. He flexed his fingers, testing the material, and then froze.
The floor was vibrating beneath his feet.
There was a constant low hum, almost like a distant magical engine thrumming in the air. Frey’s tail flicked, brushing against the strange bedding, and he stood cautiously, glancing around the room. His horns were still there, but fewer adornments than usual clung to them. He could still feel his body, his physical self, but the sense of disconnection gnawed at him.
"Where am I?" he muttered, stepping across the small room. He felt for any clues. A small handle embedded in the wall revealed a wardrobe filled with more of the same strange suits—except for one, a shirt that seemed to be made entirely of interwoven threads, leaving very little to the imagination. Not helpful, he thought, closing the wardrobe.
A shelf behind a sleek, unfamiliar mirror held two toothbrushes, tucked away as if they’d been used. Frey frowned. Someone else had been—or was—here. A companion? Jun?
A shimmer of unease ran through him as his eyes scanned the room again. There was no window, no natural light. Only smooth, grey surfaces and the constant, thrumming vibration. His heart raced slightly, and he reached instinctively for his magic. A simple cantrip, just to test—
Nothing.
His heart dropped. The connection to his magic was gone. He tried again, focusing harder this time, but there was no response. No warmth, no flicker of arcane energy. He was cut off. Frey swore under his breath. This is bad.
His hands brushed against the smooth wall, and as he did, his fingers found something—a strange panel, its surface dotted with glowing symbols. Hesitant, but driven by curiosity, Frey pressed one.
A faint ssshnnkk sound filled the room, and the wall slid to the side, revealing a corridor beyond. The thrumming grew louder, echoing down the metallic hallway.
“Huh,” Frey muttered to himself. “Definitely sorcery.” He stepped cautiously out of the room, still on edge. His mind raced as he tried to make sense of it all. Where was Jun? Was this some kind of trap, or had he been transported to another world entirely?
The sound of footsteps caught his attention. He whirled, ready for a fight—until he recognized the figure walking toward him.
“Fizzy?” Frey’s voice rose in surprise.
The woman turned, her face lighting up with a smile. She was covered in dark stains, her blue overalls worn and dirty, a far cry from the pristine noble’s daughter he had once known. Her hair was tied back in a messy braid, and she was fiddling with a strange device in her hands.
“‘Sup, Frey?” she said casually, glancing up. “Something you need?”
Frey blinked in disbelief, his mind reeling. He hadn’t seen Fizzy in... how long had it been? Before he could stop himself, his legs moved on instinct, and he pulled her into a tight hug.
“I’m so happy to see you!” Frey said, his voice full of genuine relief. Fizzy stiffened at first, then returned the hug cautiously, her eyes darting around nervously.
“Uh… you okay?” she asked, pulling back and giving him an odd look. “You seem… different.”
Frey laughed, trying to shake off the weirdness of it all. “Never better! Have you seen Jun?” he asked, hope rising in his chest.
The change in Fizzy’s expression was instant. Her face darkened, eyes narrowing as she stepped back, her body tensing. “He’s in the cargo bay,” she said, her voice flat, suddenly guarded.
Frey’s smile faltered, but he forced himself to stay positive. “Great! I’ll just… head there then.” He glanced around, scanning the corridor for any indication of direction. Panels lined the walls, but none of it made sense.
As he turned his back to her, he didn’t hear the soft, almost inaudible click of a weapon being drawn.
Suddenly, a sharp crack of electricity arced through his body. His limbs seized up, and with a muffled gasp, Frey crumpled to the floor. His entire body felt like it had been hit by a lightning bolt—his muscles numb, his magic still unresponsive.
From his place on the floor, Frey could barely see Fizzy’s face, her expression filled with shock and terror.
“Star! Brian Styles!” she yelled, her voice shaky. “I need help!”
The world around Frey dimmed as his vision blurred. The last thing he saw before everything went dark was Fizzy, standing over him with fear etched into her features. But something else lingered in her eyes—something that chilled Frey to his core. Anger.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Frey’s arms throbbed with pain as he slowly regained consciousness. His head was heavy, and the world felt hazy and distorted. Voices filtered through the fog.
“He’s waking up,” came a voice—familiar, but with an edge of tension.
“Jun, you should probably leave,” another voice urged, wary.
“No,” a third voice—sharp, angry. That one was Jun’s.
Frey shook his head, trying to clear the cobwebs, but the motion only made the ache in his neck worse. He opened his eyes slowly, and what he saw sent a chill through his entire body. He was bound tightly, arms pulled behind him, legs tied together, and even a strap around his neck tethered him to the wall. He couldn’t move an inch.
Standing before him were faces he knew—faces he trusted and had thought of as friends: Brian Styles, Star, Fizzy, and… Jun.
“Jun…” Frey breathed, his voice laced with both relief and confusion. Something was horribly wrong here. They all stared at him, but their expressions weren’t ones of concern or compassion. No, their eyes were filled with suspicion, cold anger, and hostility. Jun, in particular, looked furious, his fingers crackling with barely contained lightning.
“I’m going to give you one chance,” Jun growled, his voice sharp and menacing in a way Frey had never heard before. “Get out of that body.”
The words hit Frey like a punch to the gut. His heart raced as the reality of the situation settled in. This wasn’t just a misunderstanding—these people thought he was someone, or something, else. And Jun… Jun was ready to kill him if he said the wrong thing.
He took a shaky breath. He had to stay calm, had to be careful. One wrong move and things could go south fast. “Jun… wait, just listen. It’s me—”
A jolt of lightning shot from Jun’s fingertips, surging through Frey’s body. Agony coursed through him, making him scream. His muscles seized, his body writhing against the restraints. Tears blurred his vision, and he gasped for breath as the pain subsided for just a moment.
“Jun,” Fizzy said softly, stepping forward and placing a hand on Jun’s wrist, her voice careful. “That’s Frey’s body.”
Jun didn’t even look at her, his gaze fixed darkly on Frey. “Frey and I talked about this. This is what he wanted if he was taken again.” Without a glance, he flicked his fingers again, and another shockwave of pain ripped through Frey’s body. The sensation was unbearable, and he let out another scream.
“I’m Frey! I’m Frey!” Frey shouted through the pain, his voice desperate. “But… but I’m not your Frey!”
The lightning stopped abruptly. The tension in the room shifted as Jun’s gaze narrowed. His anger didn’t fade, but there was a flicker of curiosity now. “Explain. Now.”
Frey’s chest heaved as he struggled to breathe, the pain still radiating through his limbs. His throat was raw from the screams, and tears streaked his face. He had no choice but to tell them everything. His only hope was that they’d believe him.
“I’m… I’m not from here,” Frey gasped, his voice strained. “I’m from a different realm.”
Jun’s eyes remained hard, but he cocked his head slightly, waiting. “Go on.”
“I met you,” Frey continued, swallowing the lump in his throat. “You four. In a place called Saltmarsh. We travelled together. We became friends. And then—then last night, Jun—my Jun—vanished. We found out he’d fallen through a barrier, into another world. And I followed him… I followed him here to bring him back.”
Frey’s vision swam as he looked at them, his body still trembling from the lingering effects of Jun’s magic. “Please. Please believe me. I’m not here to hurt anyone. I just want to find my friend.”
There was silence for a long moment. Frey’s heart pounded in his chest, the weight of their eyes on him suffocating. Jun’s expression remained guarded, but the anger had simmered just a little.
“How do we know you’re telling the truth?” Brian Styles asked quietly, but his voice carried the weight of the group’s doubt. “If you’re not from here, then why are you in Frey’s body? How did that happen?”
“I don’t know,” Frey admitted, his voice hoarse. “When I stepped through the barrier, everything became… chaos. I must’ve ended up here in your Frey’s place. I don’t know how it works—none of this makes sense to me either.” He looked at Jun, pleading with his eyes. “But I swear, I’m telling the truth. I’m Frey, just… not the one you know.”
Jun studied him for a long moment, the crackling magic in his fingertips finally fading. His face was still hard, but there was a flicker of something else there—conflict.
“You’re not my Frey,” Jun said, his voice low, a dangerous edge still in his tone. “So where is he?”
Frey shook his head, his throat tightening with emotion. “I don’t know. I didn’t know this would happen, I’m just looking for my Jun. When I find him I’ll leave again.”
Star crossed his arms, glancing at Jun. “We’ve seen some strange things before, Jun. What if he’s telling the truth?”
Jun remained silent, his eyes never leaving Frey’s face. Frey held his breath, praying that somehow, someway, they would believe him. He had nothing left but the truth.
Finally, after what felt like an eternity, Jun lowered his hand, though the suspicion hadn’t left his gaze.
“If you’re lying…” Jun’s voice was a quiet, cold threat. “I’ll make sure you regret it.”
Frey swallowed hard, his body aching and weak. “I’m not lying,” he whispered. “I just need your help.”
Another heavy silence settled over the room, but this time, the hostility seemed to have lessened, even if only slightly. Frey knew he wasn’t out of danger yet, but at least he wasn’t being shocked into oblivion anymore.
For now, that was enough.

Chapter Four
Frey found himself back in the small, confining cabin where he had first awoken. The walls felt more suffocating now as he desperately pressed every glowing rune and symbol on the panel by the door, hoping for some kind of release. But no matter how many times he tried, the door remained sealed shut. He was trapped.
Prisoner, his mind whispered. He clenched his fists, frustration boiling within him. How was he supposed to find his Jun if he was stuck in here, cut off from everything?
With little else to do, Frey forced himself to think through the events that had just unfolded. The confrontation with this world's version of Jun and the others played over in his mind. It was a small relief to know that in this realm, Fizzy, Brian Styles, and Star were together, seemingly unharmed, and that they cared deeply for their Frey. The fact that their Frey was important to them should have comforted him, but the memory of Jun’s fierce, almost predatory eyes left him shaken.
That wasn’t his Jun.
This Jun was someone darker, someone forged in different fires—someone who could become a threat. Frey remembered Rayra’s words: The Jun in this realm would be different. She had warned him. Frey was in the body of another version of himself, but what had happened to this world’s Frey? Had he somehow suppressed him? Was the other Frey now in Saltmarsh, trying to navigate his life?
Frey closed his eyes, forcing himself to focus. He reached inward, feeling for his magic, but was only met with the cold emptiness where it should have been. The void made his stomach clench. He pushed past it, concentrating deeper, searching for a presence—any sign of the Frey whose body he now occupied.
Hello? he thought cautiously. Are you here, Frey?
For a moment, there was only silence. Then, a voice—his own voice—echoed back to him.
Finally! the voice exclaimed, making Frey startle in surprise.
Are you Frey? Frey asked tentatively.
A positive affirmation hummed in response.
Relief washed over him in a wave. I’m sorry I’ve taken your body, he began, guilt threading through his thoughts, but the other Frey interrupted him.
It’s okay. I can see your memories. We’re doing this for Jun.
Frey nearly wept from the release of tension. This world’s Frey wasn’t angry, wasn’t trying to fight him for control. He understood. And he was with him. But beneath that understanding, Frey felt something else. A flicker of emotion, something heavier, lingering between the lines of their mental connection.
He hesitated, then asked, Are you and Jun… more?
The voice in his head chuckled softly. This is our bedroom.
Frey’s eyes widened as he looked around the small cabin again, his gaze falling on the bright lavender bedspread. He saw it now, the detail in the embroidered patterns, the way the room had a strangely intimate feel. This Frey and this Jun were together? Frey blinked, his mind spinning.
As he processed this revelation, he felt the other Frey observing him, an amused undercurrent in their shared thoughts.
Frey turned his gaze inward, sifting through his own feelings. Jun was his friend, someone he had fiercely protected, someone who had become an anchor in the chaotic world they had faced together. He had always admired Jun’s persistence, his courage, even in the face of self-doubt. There was something so endearing about the way Jun constantly second-guessed himself, how unsure he seemed in his own skin. Frey had felt that protectiveness—an instinct to keep Jun safe—but now, as he reflected, he realised there was more.
The way Jun’s violet eyes caught the moonlight during their late-night watches. The way his jaw clenched when he was focused, determined, lost in thought. The quiet gratitude in his smile when Frey handed him a waterskin during their journey. The feeling of Jun’s lips on his as they shared a breath of air… The warmth that had spread through Frey’s chest at those small moments.
Oh. Frey’s thoughts echoed with sudden clarity. OH.
The voice in his head let out a gleeful laugh. This is brilliant! You didn’t even know! it crooned, amusement bubbling from the other Frey. You’ve been travelling together all this time, and you had no idea!
Frey shook his head, his face growing warm. How was I supposed to know? he protested. We’ve been running from one disaster to another since I met them! We’ve barely had time to breathe, let alone think about… He trailed off, his thoughts spinning with realisation.
Feelings? the other Frey teased, clearly enjoying his inner turmoil.
Frey huffed, feeling both embarrassed and overwhelmed. It’s not like I’ve had a moment to figure out anything!
But now that it was out there, now that he had put words to the attraction that had simmered beneath the surface for so long, Frey couldn’t unsee it. His relationship with Jun—his Jun—was more than just friendship, more than just comradeship on the battlefield. There had always been something deeper, but he had been too focused on the mission, too caught up in survival, to recognise it.
Well, now you know, the other Frey said, his voice gentle but teasing. But what are you going to do about it?
Frey sat back on the bed, overwhelmed. He had crossed into another realm to bring Jun back, and in doing so, he had uncovered not just a fractured reality, but a truth about his own heart. He wasn’t sure what to do next, but one thing was clear: he couldn’t leave Jun behind. Not this Jun, not his Jun.
I need to find him, Frey thought firmly, more to himself than to the other Frey. I need to bring him home.
The other Frey was silent for a moment, then offered a simple response: Then we’ll do it together.
Frey's thoughts churned with the possibility. There’s a chance that my Jun is sharing the same body as your Jun, just like we’re sharing, he mused, trying to make sense of it all. Do you think your Jun is any different?
There was a pause, as though the other Frey was carefully considering the question. Then the voice in his head responded, From what I’ve seen, he reacted pretty much as expected.
Frey laid his head back, staring at the metal plates forming the ceiling. But he seemed so… He searched for the right word. Scary.
Another pause, and this time, Frey could feel the other Frey choosing his words with care. We’ve had a rough few years. We’ve all suffered, but I think Jun feels like he has to carry the responsibility for it.
You’ve been together for years? Frey’s eyes widened as the weight of that realisation hit him. I’ve got some catching up to do! He chuckled to himself, but then a new thought crept into his mind. Wait… where are we anyway? This place doesn’t look like any building I’ve ever seen. And why can’t I use my magic?
There was a sudden burst of indignant spluttering from the other Frey. What the fuck?! the voice exclaimed, disbelief heavy in its tone. You can do magic!?
Frey couldn't help but laugh at the shock in the other Frey’s voice. Yes, of course! Fireball, prestidigitation—the usual. I’d even argue I’m more reliable than Jun when it comes to using it.
The silence that followed was heavy, and Frey could feel the other him processing this information with quiet astonishment. The connection between them seemed to thrum with mixed emotions—curiosity, envy, and a touch of awe.
I can’t believe it… the other Frey muttered.
Frey, intrigued by the differences between their realms, gave the other Frey some time to process. So… where are we, anyway? he asked, eager to steer the conversation back to the strange place they were in.
We’re on a spaceship, the other Frey said simply.
Frey blinked, stunned into silence for the first time since this entire ordeal had begun. A… spaceship? He had been expecting something fantastical—a sorcerer’s tower, maybe, or some other magical prison. But this?
The other Frey’s thoughts were tinged with amusement. Yeah, a spaceship. Welcome to the future, or at least, what we call home.
Frey’s mind reeled. He hadn’t even considered that the realms he might visit could be so drastically different. Spaceships? he thought incredulously. He felt a wave of warmth from the other Frey, who seemed to be quietly enjoying his surprise.
We’ve got a bit of time, the other Frey said. Let’s catch up.
Frey laughed, his astonishment turning into a grin. I think I’m going to need a minute to wrap my head around this, he admitted, sitting up on the bed. Okay, tell me everything. What’s life like here? What’s Jun like?
The other Frey’s voice softened as he began to recount their lives. Well, for starters, magic is rare here. Jun’s renowned for being a sorcerer, he’s quite powerful. As to their reaction to this possession, well, a few years back I messed with a trinket and a dangerous creature took over my body. It… hurt us. Hurt Jun. We vowed not to let it happen again. Then more trouble happened, we were attacked. Star and I were captured, Brian Styles was blown up… The others thought we were dead. It’s a miracle we managed to make it back together, but we have scars, we always will.I think that’s why you saw him so… guarded. He’s had to be strong for all of us.
Frey listened closely, fascinated by the details. He remembered his Jun, driven by a fierce need to protect his friends, the guilt and helplessness he showed when he couldn’t save everyone. The memories flashed behind his eyes.
Yeah, that definitely seems like him, the other Frey agreed.
So what, do we just, what, talk to him? Frey asked, suddenly feeling a little overwhelmed by indecision. He’d jumped on this task with no clear idea how to accomplish it, or even how to get back home once he had.
I guess so? Once they’ve had time to adjust then we’ll speak to Jun and get a clearer idea of whether he’s alone up in there. The other Frey replied, as if sensing his worry, it will be okay. I’m here to help.
Frey smiled, and settled down to wait.
It was around an hour later when the door buzzed and the panel slid open, revealing Star. He still wore large gauntlets and seemed uneasy, but he beckoned Frey up.
“You still you?” He asked gruffly, Frey made a show of studying his limbs.
“Who else would I be?” He asked with a raised eyebrow. Star huffed,
“I wouldn’t be a smart ass if I were you. You’re on thin ice already. Now come on.” He turned and left, leaving Frey confused. He followed.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Star led Frey into the dining room, where a large table occupied the centre. The table's surface bore numerous scrapes, scratches, and stains—testaments to years of use, not only as a dining area but as a gathering place for all kinds of activities.
Around the table, Fizzy, Brian Styles, and Jun were already seated. Steaming plates of strange dumplings and unfamiliar vegetables sat before each of them—except Brian Styles, who was busy scribbling in a notebook. Two empty places awaited; Star took one and gestured briskly for Frey to take the other.
Frey sat down gratefully, eyeing the food in front of him. It was nothing like the hearty fare he was used to in Saltmarsh; meat platters and thick broths, yet the aroma was enticing. Glancing around, he let his gaze linger on Jun, who ate quietly, avoiding eye contact. Fizzy, however, gave him a warm, curious smile.
“So, Frey,” she began, “what’s it like in the universe you came from?” Frey could tell she was testing him, but he relished the chance to talk about his world to an attentive audience.
“Well, where to start? Our group is pretty wild.” He chuckled. “I was the last to join. My friend Eddie—”
“You know Eddie?” Fizzy interrupted, her tone surprised. The others paused, utensils mid-air. Only the steady scratch-scratch of Brian’s pen filled the silence. Frey nodded eagerly.
“Eddie and I go way back. He rescued me when I was young, kind of a father figure. He always did right by me. He travelled with the group for a while before settling his caravan in Saltmarsh, we think he’s going to get into politics to improve the town.”
Star scowled. “Doesn’t sound like our Eddie.”
Curious but knowing Eddie wasn’t the main focus, Frey continued, realising honesty was his best proof of who he was.
“Eddie invited me to visit. I was intrigued, and you guys seemed exciting. I stayed with you and we visited a wizard’s tower that led us into the fae realm. It was there that, well… we lost our Fizzy. She was taken over by some spirit called Gavin.” Frey’s voice faltered. The scratching of Brian’s pen stopped, and everyone stared. “We’re still looking for her,” he added quietly, his gaze dropping to his untouched food. A soft hand touched his; he looked up to see Fizzy giving him a gentle smile.
“I didn’t get to know you that well,” he said to her, “but everyone’s determined to find you. Jun especially took it hard.”
“What happened next?” Star prompted.
Frey gathered himself. “Jun was struggling the whole time we were in the fae realm—he’s part fae, apparently.” Jun raised an eyebrow, and the others gave him curious looks. “Anyway, we killed a dragon, freed some cyclops, travelled to a mushroom land filled with walking corpses, killed a necromancer, and even saved some sentient trees before leaving. After that, Star told us we needed to go to his home in the Rokkoss Mountains to stop the sun from being destroyed.” Star nodded thoughtfully, the name obviously ringing familiarly to him. “We headed north, met Star’s friend Ernie, and climbed the mountain, slaying yetis, hags, and giants along the way. When we finally reached his village, we learned we each represented an element: Star was air, Brian Styles was water, Jun was earth, and I was fire.”
He paused, taking a breath. “We went to sleep after all that, and when I woke, Jun was gone, without a trace.”
“Holy crap,” Fizzy breathed. “So… you guys do a lot of killing?”
Frey grinned sheepishly. “Yeah, we’re a solid team. Star and Brian are our front-line hitters, and Jun and I support with magic.” He glanced at Jun. “I’m more offensive with fireballs, and Jun, well… he supports in his own way.”
Jun’s eyes narrowed. “You can use magic?”
Frey blinked, feeling self-conscious under Jun’s scrutiny. “Uh, yeah. Magic’s pretty common where I’m from. Star’s got a sword that summons ghosts, and Brian Styles is actually a magical construct made from an old boat.” He paused, then smirked. “But your magic’s different—you sometimes get these random surges, either really powerful or… interesting. We think it’s because you’re a fairy.”
Jun’s expression darkened, but before he could retort, Star laughed. “Ha! I always said you were a delicate fairy, Jun. This proves it.”
Jun exhaled sharply. “Fine. Anyway, how do we get our Frey back?”
His question startled Frey. Then he remembered. “Oh, he’s still here! In me. It’s like we’re sharing consciousness.”
The room seemed to grow colder as Jun went still, a guarded look flashing in his eyes. Fizzy bit her lip.
“But he’s okay, right?” she asked quickly.
“Oh, absolutely! We had a great chat earlier.” Frey assured her, then he became sombre, “He told me about the last time his body was taken over, but he said this is nothing like that.” Frey put his hands up in a calming gesture. “Actually, I wondered if it was the same for you, Jun. My Jun was asleep until I, well, focused and ‘woke’ him up. Maybe yours is there, too?”
Jun’s gaze hardened. “Prove it. Let him out.”
Frey nodded. “Right, give me a sec.” He closed his eyes, focusing inward. Frey? he called. Can you help me out here?
A familiar, reassuring voice responded. Sure thing. Won’t be long.
Frey opened his eyes, feeling slightly disoriented. The air had shifted; Jun now looked at him with a softened expression, relief visible in the set of his face. Fizzy and Brian shared a look of quiet reassurance, and Star appeared lost in thought.
“Did he speak?” Frey asked, already knowing the answer. Fizzy grinned, turning to Jun.
“Okay, your turn! Let’s see if there’s a Jun Number Two hiding somewhere up there!”
Jun set down his cutlery and closed his eyes, fingertips pressed together in concentration. A minute passed. Then two. Frey shifted uncomfortably, eyeing the now-lukewarm dumplings. Finally giving in, he took a bite and continued eating as the silence stretched on.
By the time he finished his meal and drained the tea Brian had quietly placed in front of him, Jun opened his eyes.
“Nothing,” he said flatly, a touch of sorrow in his voice.
“Are you sure?” Star asked, brows furrowing. “Your head is pretty scatty, maybe he’s hiding?”
Jun’s scowl returned. “I’m sure. Sorry, Frey. You mentioned different realms—your Jun must be in another one.”
Frey nodded, disappointment flickering across his face. “That’s fine. It would’ve been too easy if I found Jun in the first portal. I’ll leave as soon as I figure out how.”
Actually, I think I might know how! his alternate self spoke up, a hint of excitement in his voice. There’s a doorway in here—I don’t really want to go near it, but I’m pretty sure it wasn’t there before. If you open it, you might be able to leave!
Frey perked up, grasping at the idea, even if it felt tenuous. “Better than nothing!” he said aloud, though the optimism in his voice felt forced. He glanced around and realised he’d spoken out loud without meaning to. They were watching him with curious expressions.
“Uh… your Frey has an idea I’m going to try,” he explained, a little sheepishly. “If it works, I’ll be gone.”
Suddenly, a wave of unexpected emotion washed over him as he looked at each of them—their familiar faces tinged with subtle differences, marked by experiences he didn’t fully understand. His gaze lingered on Jun. This Jun seemed worn down, his warmth hidden beneath a hard, almost bitter edge. Frey vowed quietly to himself that, whatever it took, he’d protect his own Jun from ending up this way.
“It was nice meeting you,” he said softly, sincerity lacing his words. He closed his eyes, focusing on the image of the door his alternate self had described. Slowly, he reached for it, imagining his hand on a handle just out of reach.
And then, as he grasped it, he felt a pull—like stepping off a ledge. The world tilted, and he fell through.
